utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish good afternoon to everyone here present as well as to the public gallery. If Madam Registrar would be kindly -- kind enough to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-41-PT, the Prosecutor versus Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, ma'am. I would kindly ask the parties to introduce themselves for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Mark Harmon appearing for the Office of the Prosecutor. To my right is Ms. Magda Karagiannakis and to her right Mr. Fergal Gaynor and to my right Ms. Donnica Henry Frijlink, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, counsel. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am Tomislav Jonjic, Defence counsel for the accused Pasko Ljubicic, and here is my co-counsel Mrs. Nika Pinter, attorney-at-law from Zagreb, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, counsel. I should like to remind you that this Status Conference was convened according to Article 65 bis of the Statute to discuss the main problems that have to be reviewed before the beginning of the trial. I do not need to remind you that the objectives at which this Article 65 bis is aimed is to ensure a speedy preparation for the trial but also at giving the accused the opportunity to express himself by raising the issues to which he would like to draw the attention of the Tribunal such as his health condition. I would, therefore, like to ask Mr. Ljubicic whether he can hear me in a language he understands.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you perfectly. As for my health, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm going to interrupt you. Later on during the hearing we will have much more time to discuss that. You can now sit down. I should like to remind you that this is our fifth Status Conference in this case. We convened the last time on the 23rd of May, and I believe that it is now time to move forward without wasting more time. I would like to finalise today certain outstanding issues. I have established a schedule for this Status Conference, and I have, myself, identified four items to be discussed, but I also invite the parties to raise any additional issue without hesitation should they feel that is necessary. The first item is the state of communications concerning disclosure of documents between parties. The second item is the situation in the matter of disclosure of documents containing elements of evidence on the part of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The third item is the pending, still pending, investigation regarding the transcripts from other cases under Article 82 -- 92 bis of the Rules of Procedure. And the fourth item is to attempt to make an estimate as to the duration of the trial, including the number the witnesses. Therefore, we will later have an opportunity to hear from Mr. Ljubicic. Do the parties have any issue to add to this agenda? I should like to ask the Prosecutor to take the floor first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have none. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And Mr. Jonjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has nothing either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, counsel. So shall we begin with the first item which concerns the disclosure of evidence under Article 65 -- 66, Rule 66. I have received today a transcript of a session held yesterday between the two parties under Rule 65 ter. Through the good offices of Mr. Harhoff, Senior Legal Officer, I would like to make sure that I have properly understood the situation. The Prosecutor has confirmed that he has completed disclosure of evidence accompanying, supporting the indictment. That is one. Second, the Prosecutor has disclosed, under Rule 66 (ii), copies of all witness statements of all witnesses that are intended to be called, as well as all the statements taken under Rule 92. But I have remarked that the Prosecution intends to invite other witnesses apart from those initially listed, and the Prosecution is referring to one, two, or perhaps more witnesses. Is the Prosecution not able to give us a final number and the identity of these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have identified two witnesses. We are conducting a mission to interview one of those witnesses, I believe, next week. We will make an assessment as to whether that witness has information that would be valuable to the Trial Chamber, and if we conclude that his evidence is information that the Trial Chamber should hear, we will identify him as a witness for the trial, and we will submit his statement immediately to the Defence. Likewise, in -- on the week of the -- the second week of October, we will be interviewing another witness who we have identified, and the same applies to that witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I have understood correctly, it is all in all two additional witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct. There is a third witness, but I cannot go into details as to that witness at this particular hearing. So there are three potential new witnesses, two of whom we will be interviewing, a third I cannot, at this point in time, discuss in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you wish later, perhaps, to into private session for that or do you prefer to postpone this altogether until the next conference, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be preparing written submissions that will address the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It has been brought to my attention that there are pending motions filed on the 8th of September, and it is identification -- the Prosecutor's notification concerning two witnesses. So in addition to the three I have identified just a moment ago, there is before the Court the motion that is pending concerning two witnesses, but the Court has already that information before it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two out of the three or two plus three?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And on the part of the Defence, are there any remarks to be made on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We see no need to add to what we said at yesterday's session, yesterday's 65 ter hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, counsel, but there is, nevertheless, one issue that is a bit of a concern to me. If I understood correctly, you raised yesterday the issue of translation. You said you received documents that were not translated. Is this matter settled or have you settled anything with the Prosecution? Do you have an agreement with them that these documents will be translated within an acceptable time frame?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There is between the Prosecution and the Defence team a difference regarding the list of disclosed documents and their translation into a language the accused understands. I received a letter today from Mr. Harmon in which he suggests a way in which to solve this matter. I cannot tell you anything precise about whether translations will be available to the Defence, because we have received these documents on a CD-ROM, and that requires more time for review and comparison. So I stand by my suggestion made yesterday, and that is that the Defence will very shortly inform Mr. Harmon and Mr. Harhoff about the status of this translation, and I believe we will settle this matter very soon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, counsel. I am very happy to hear that there is a communication between the parties and a goodwill to find agreement. There is a minor point, counsel, that I should like to know more about, namely, do you reckon on availing yourself of the opportunity to apply Rule 66(B)?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has not yet made a final decision on this issue in view of the fact that, as I said, we received a great amount of material on CD-ROM, but we will make a decision shortly after we have reviewed this. We will simply be able to judge very soon whether we will need to do that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, counsel. Very well. I am now speaking to Mr. Harmon. Where are we as to the application of Rule 68 exculpatory material?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday Ms. Karagiannakis supplied a report on our efforts to comply fully with Rule 68. I'm prepared to turn the floor over to Ms. Karagiannakis and she can expand if necessary on what she said yesterday in the 65 ter conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I would have liked to hear, as usual, the status of this disclosure, briefly if you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's happy to report that we've made substantial progress on the Rule 68 disclosure. The -- we have reviewed the two main archives that should contain information relevant to this case, those being the archives of the ABiH and also the Croatian archives. In respect of the archives of the ABiH, we created a spreadsheet containing the Rule 68 documents and also gave those documents plus the entire archive to the Defence in searchable CD-ROM fashion so they are able not only to see the documents that we've identified as Rule 68 but also able to search the archive themselves to find any other material they may think is relevant to the conduct of their defence. This was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to interrupt you, but isn't disclosure of everything to the Defence a way to avoid all these complications?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the jurisprudence of this court requires us to identify Rule 68 material, and we have done so by providing a separate smaller spreadsheet, not of all the material but of the material that has been identified by us as Rule 68. We've just given the remainder of the material to them just in case they want to search it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: That was provided to the Defence on the 18th of September. In relation to the Croatian archives, a search has been made. Rule 68 documents have been identified. Those documents were burnt onto CD-ROM and given -- disclosed to the Defence today. We have also a third category of documents that we've looked at and that is statements. On the 10th of September, we disclosed ten statements under Rule 68 to the Defence and hopefully this afternoon or tomorrow morning we will be in a position to disclose an additional eight or ten additional statements to the Defence under the Rule. Finally, we have also conducted, through our own research for the preparation of this case, searches and identified 31 documents which -- which could fall under the ambit of Rule 68, and they were disclosed in hard copy to the Defence on the 18th of September. The issue -- that is our Rule 68 disclosure as it stands today. Obviously Rule 68 is an ongoing obligation, and the Prosecutor will continue to search for relevant materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. Very well. We shall then pass to the second item that I would like, nevertheless, to ask Madam Registrar to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Are we in open session? Thank you. The third issue that I would like to raise is the request concerning the admission of transcripts from other cases pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. If I have understood this correctly, this matter was discussed yesterday by the parties, and the parties are still in disagreement. The Defence stands by its position, namely, it quite simply dismisses this request made by the Prosecution. Mr. Jonjic, is it your position that these transcripts, this testimony, has direct results, direct consequences on the conduct of the accused? Is this a matter of law are you raising or is it a matter of convenience? I would like to be clear on this point. Does this -- is this a matter of public interest in this case or are you saying that it is contrary to the letter and the spirit of Rule 92 bis and that the Trial Chamber should dismiss the Prosecution's request? I'm not certain about this. What is your position exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence replied on the 18th of July, 2003, a reply to the motion of the Prosecution and stated the reasons for which it was against having these transcripts admitted. As discussed at the meeting yesterday, the 65 ter meeting, the Defence stands by its position and holds that in the case of all the transcripts suggested in the Prosecution's request, the matters at stake concerned the Prosecution's case in an essential manner. And by admitting these transcripts, we would violate the accused's right to a fair defence which are guaranteed by the Tribunal Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Defence counsel considers that the accused's right to cross-examine witnesses is one of his fundamental rights, which must by no means be violated, not at any cost. Especially not in order to expedite the affair. On the other hand, the Defence is aware that by admitting these transcripts, the accused's right to cross-examination would be restricted. And given that this is a matter of testimony that concerned the conduct of the accused quite directly or the conduct of persons who in the amended indictment were subordinate to him, the Defence counsel considers that in such a case, his right to a fair trial would be violated. This is why we are against admitting these transcripts. But if the Trial Chamber decides that they should be admitted, then it is the Defence's position that all the testimony given by these witnesses before this Tribunal should be admitted, all the testimony given in other cases and not just the testimony suggested by the Prosecutor in his submission. The reason for this is that a number of witnesses listed in the Prosecution's submission testified with regard to various cases over a long period of time. Circumstances have changed in the meantime. Many facts have come to light, much evidence has come to light which casts a different light on this testimony. In other cases, the Defence was not in a position or perhaps was not interested in cross-examining witnesses in such a manner. In the present situation, the Defence holds that is in a position to put questions which would not only cast doubt on the credibility but would also significantly affect their contribution to establishing the truth in this case. An additional reason is that these witnesses were examined in other cases in which the accused did not necessarily have the same interests, and I'm using an euphemism. Their interests were not the same as the accused Ljubicic. So for the sake of protecting the interests of the accused and to establish truth, we believe that witnesses should come before the Trial Chamber and be cross-examined both by the Prosecution and by the Defence. The time that would be saved in this way, by admitting these transcripts, by accepting the Prosecution's request, is not significant in the Defence's opinion, and we therefore don't think that the rights of the accused should be violated for the sake of saving time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jonjic, but I must remind you about two or three points. I would like to draw your attention to Rule 92 bis (D), to the wording of that Rule, and my question concerns this Rule, because paragraph (D) says, and I quote: "A Chamber may admit a transcript of evidence given by a witness in proceedings before the Tribunal which goes to proof of a matter other than the acts and conduct of the accused." My question is: Are you raising this objection on the grounds that the testimony attempts to prove an issue that directly concerns an act or the conduct of the accused, or are you demanding that these witnesses be cross-examined?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as it says in the Defence's response to this submission, the Defence's position is that the testimony of the witnesses whose -- for whom you want to admit the transcripts concern the conduct and the acts of the accused since he was accused on the basis of command and responsibility and on his individual responsibility although his name may not be directly mentioned, this concerns testimonies that concern him directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your opinion, the Prosecution's demand violates the letter and the spirit of paragraph (D) of Rule 92 bis (D); is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to hear what the Prosecution has to say about this matter very briefly, please. Do you approve of the position of the Defence to the extent that the Defence says that this testimony has to do with the direct acts and conduct of the accused? Do you agree with this? And therefore, it would be a matter of violating the letter and the spirit of paragraph (D) under Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the benefit of my pleadings that I filed in this particular aspect of the case before me, but we filed these fully aware of the existence of 92 bis (D) which says that such written evidence is inadmissible if it goes to the acts or conduct of the accused. After analysing the statements, we concluded a certain number of pieces of -- a number of statements that would not run afoul of 92 bis (D), and therefore we submitted those statements and a motion to seek their admission under the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are claiming that this does not contradict, it doesn't violate letter or the spirit of this Rule. But I would also like you to respond to what the Defence claimed. If you are demanding that certain witness transcripts be admitted in such case -- in such a case, then you should request that all the transcripts of witnesses. Is your position one that is in agreement with that of the Defence, or do you have any objections to raise to this suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, my response, Your Honour, is such a response is premature. First of all, the Trial Chamber has not ruled on the admission of these statements under Rule 92 bis. My second observation is 92 bis applies to the Defence as well and should there be portions of transcripts of other cases that it wishes to have considered by the Trial Chamber, it can, at the appropriate time, make a motion seeking admission of portions of other transcripts of other proceedings. The admission of all of the transcripts from all of the proceedings, I think, would be unduly burdensome on the Chamber, because I am fully aware that some of these witnesses have testified in cases that have absolutely no bearing on the events in Central Bosnia, and to burden the Chamber with the admission of all of those transcripts and the burden of going through those, I think, would be time-consuming and needlessly not helpful to the issues that will be before the Court. So my position at this point is, one, we should wait to see what happens to the application made by the Prosecutor in respect of these 12 witnesses to see if the written evidence is admitted; two, if it is, the Defence can avail itself to 92 bis (D) and seek admission of testimony or relevant portions of these witnesses' testimony in other proceedings; and three, I would oppose, at this point in time, the admission of all of the transcripts of all of the previous testimonies of all of these witnesses no matter what proceeding it took place in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. I think I have understood your idea. It is your case. You are presenting the Prosecution's case and, therefore, within these limits you are content to present as evidence the transcripts whose admission you have requested pursuant to Rule 92 bis. But I would like to ask you, whether you are against these witnesses being cross-examined by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think that is a -- no, I am not is the first answer and the direct answer to your question. I think it's up to the Trial Chamber to make an assessment as to whether cross-examination, under the circumstances of this case, is something that would aid the Trial Chamber. I have no objections to those witnesses being called before this Chamber and being cross-examined, but I think, ultimately, it's for the Trial Chamber to make a decision whether such cross-examination would be beneficial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think at this stage, if I've understood this correctly, the Defence is requesting that these witness be cross-examined. So I will move onto the fourth item, namely the duration of the trial, the estimate for the duration of the trial. I suggest the following schedule: In my opinion, a period of two months should be quite sufficient for the Prosecution to make its case, and a month and a half is granted to make submissions for demands of acquittal in accordance with 98 bis of the Rule. Two months are granted to the Defence to present its version of the facts. One week is granted for the accused to testify if he so desires, and then one week is granted for the closing arguments of the parties. I have made some calculations, and that gives a total of six months, roughly speaking. And I'm now addressing the parties: Does the Prosecution agree with such an estimate in principle?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In principle, Your Honour, we agree with the estimate. I'm agreeing on the basis that we will be in session five days a week and we will have five hours per day of available court time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Yes, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And what about the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence cannot give its view about the estimate or even your estimate except very theoretically, because we don't know what witnesses and how many witnesses will really be called by the Prosecution. I should also like to remind the Trial Chamber that under the decision on the admission of stipulated facts, a relatively great number of stipulated facts from other cases has been admitted, and this decision leaves the Defence the right to argue and challenge these adjudicated facts from other cases. If we decide to challenge some of these adjudicated facts, that would prolong the proceedings a little but not much, and I believe your estimate is pretty realistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, sir. I can conclude that roughly speaking, this time limit is reasonable. Are there any other matters that the parties would like to raise or discuss? Very well. In that case, I can see that no one has any matters to raise. I'm going to turn to Mr. Ljubicic. I would like to ask you whether there was anything at all that you would like to add or whether there are any matters you would like to raise other than those that concern your health, because if you're going to discuss your health, we could perhaps go into private session at least, or if you prefer, if everything is fine, we won't go into private session. Is there any issue you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe there's no need to go into private session. As for requests or questions, I have none at the moment. I believe my Defence team is informing me and keeping me posted of all developments in the case, and I am satisfied with their work. I have no objection to the treatment I'm getting at the Detention Unit. I am fine, and my health is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm glad to -- to hear what you have said. I'm glad to hear your observations. As far as your health is concerned, is there anything you would like to say or is everything fine? I would like to be certain that everything is fine and that you have no complaints.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On balance, everything is fine. I do have an ulcer and I suffer from asthma, but those are old complaints and they are under control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But are you being treated? Are you getting the necessary treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely everything I need I am getting at the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wish you good health. Please sit down. Thank you. I think that all I can do now is repeat that I wish the parties to continue collaborating and to address the legal officer, Mr. Harhoff, who is carefully following all the pre-trial cases. And once again, I wish you all a very good afternoon and until the next hearing perhaps. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.02 p.m.
